strengths: Addresses a well-motivated, practical problem: enabling high-resolution masked-image-model pretraining on consumer-grade GPUs for privacy-/resource-constrained biomedical labs, which is a genuine gap in current MAE tooling.

Solid engineering contribution appropriate for an Applied/Systems paper: numerically stable softmax-temperature reparameterization of AutoFocusFormer's inverse-distance interpolation, a Flash-Attention-style Triton kernel for cluster attention, and a point-based deformable cross-attention decoder that consumes multi-scale features -- these are concrete, reproducible technical improvements over the AFF backbone.

The deep-supervision analysis (effective-rank collapse diagnosis via Figure 4/5 and Eq. 3) is a nice diagnostic contribution that clearly motivates and validates an architectural choice rather than being an ad hoc addition.

The Perlin-noise masking strategy is well justified via spectral (PSD) analysis showing it better matches the natural 1/f statistics of EM images compared to random masking, and the ablation (Table 2d) supports the claimed benefit.

Comprehensive ablations (downsampling rate, masking ratio, deep supervision, masking strategy) and a resolution-scaling study (Table 1, Figure 10) give a reasonably thorough picture of the efficiency/accuracy trade-off, including practical metrics (FLOPs, VRAM, throughput) that matter for the stated use case.

The data-efficiency experiment (Figure 11) is a valuable addition showing AFFMAE generalizes much better than ViT-MAE under low-label regimes, which is directly relevant to the paper's target domain (annotation-scarce biomedical imaging).
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a single, private, in-house EM dataset with a single downstream task (FPW segmentation) and a single model scale (~22M parameters); there is no evaluation on any public benchmark, which limits reproducibility and makes it impossible for the community to verify or build on the numbers independently.

Despite explicitly critiquing SwinMAE and MixMAE in the related work as having reconciliation issues or pretrain/finetune mismatch, the paper never empirically compares against them (or any other hierarchical MIM baseline besides plain ViT-MAE), so the claimed advantage over the closest prior art is only argued qualitatively, not demonstrated quantitatively.

Performance parity claims ("matches ViT-MAE ... within 0.4% mIoU") are based on single-run numbers with no reported variance across seeds, making it hard to assess whether the small gaps (e.g., 0.6030 vs 0.6054, 0.6246 vs 0.6280) are meaningful or within noise.

The abstract's "Code available at" trails off with no URL, raising concern about whether code/data release is actually planned, which is important for reproducibility given the reliance on a private dataset and custom Triton kernels.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core adaptive/off-grid merging idea is taken directly from AutoFocusFormer (Ziwen et al., 2023); the paper's contribution is largely adapting/stabilizing this existing backbone for MAE-style pretraining plus systems-level kernel work, which is legitimate as an Applied/Systems contribution but should be framed accordingly rather than presented primarily as a new pretraining framework.

Generalizability beyond electron-microscopy imagery (e.g., other microscopy modalities, histology, or natural images) is untested, so it remains unclear whether the Perlin masking and downsampling-rate sweet spots (e.g., d_s=0.4, 50% masking) are dataset-specific tunings rather than broadly applicable defaults.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: enabling MAE-style hierarchical pretraining on consumer-grade GPUs for privacy-sensitive/data-governance-constrained biomedical settings, which is a reasonable applied/systems contribution.

Solid engineering effort: numerically stable softmax-temperature reformulation of AutoFocusFormer's inverse-power interpolation, a Flash-style Triton cluster-attention kernel, and a point-based deformable cross-attention decoder that consumes multi-scale features.
The deep-supervision analysis via Normalized Effective Rank is a nice diagnostic that convincingly demonstrates representation collapse in sparse deep stages and motivates the proposed fix.
The Perlin-noise masking strategy is well motivated by a spectral (PSD) analysis showing it better matches the 1/f statistics of EM images than random masking, and the ablation supports its benefit.
Reasonably thorough ablations of downsampling rate, masking ratio, deep supervision, and masking strategy on the chosen dataset/backbone.
weaknesses: All empirical results come from a single in-house, unreleased EM dataset and a single downstream task (FPW segmentation); no validation on any other biomedical or natural-image domain despite the introduction motivating broad applicability to 'novel biomedical regimes' and the conclusion speculating about 3D/4D imaging generalization.

AFFMAE never actually outperforms the ViT-MAE baseline in mIoU in any table (Table 1, Table 2) — it consistently underperforms by ~0.3-0.5 points; the framing around 'matches' or 'within 0.4%' is optimistic given no confidence intervals, error bars, or multiple seeds are reported to substantiate that the gap is within noise.

No comparison to the other hierarchical masked pretraining baselines explicitly discussed in Related Work (SwinMAE, MixMAE, SimMIM) even though the paper positions itself against exactly these methods' trade-offs; the only baseline is a dense ViT-MAE, which is not the most relevant efficiency-oriented competitor.

The core architectural machinery (AutoFocusFormer backbone, cluster attention, neighborhood merging) is adopted directly from prior work (Ziwen et al., 2023); the paper's genuinely novel contributions are largely engineering fixes (stable interpolation, Triton kernel, deep supervision, Perlin masking) rather than a new pretraining algorithm, which should be more clearly delineated as an applied/systems contribution rather than implied as a new architectural framework.

Reproducibility is limited: the pretraining and fine-tuning datasets (187k in-house EM scans and the FPW dataset) are not public, and although 'code available at' is mentioned, no actual link/repository is provided in the visible text, undermining verifiability of the efficiency and accuracy claims.

The downsampling rate d_s=0.4 is chosen as 'the optimal balance' based on a single ablation on one backbone size/resolution; it is unclear how sensitive this choice is across resolutions, dataset scales, or tasks, limiting confidence in the generality of the efficiency-accuracy trade-off curve shown in Figure 1.

The efficiency claims (FLOPs, VRAM, throughput) are compared against a dense ViT-MAE baseline of matched parameter count, but it is not clear the baseline was equally optimized (e.g., FlashAttention-style kernels, same mixed-precision engineering) — an unequal engineering effort between baseline and proposed method could inflate the reported speed/memory gains.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: efficient in-domain MAE-style pretraining on consumer-grade GPUs for privacy-sensitive/institutionally constrained biomedical imaging settings, which is a meaningful applied/systems contribution.

Sound and well-motivated technical adaptations of AutoFocusFormer to the MAE regime: a numerically stable softmax-temperature reformulation replacing the fragile inverse-power interpolation, and a FlashAttention-style Triton kernel for cluster attention that avoids materializing full attention matrices, improving mixed-precision robustness.

Deep supervision is empirically justified via a clear diagnostic (Normalized Effective Rank and PCA visualizations) showing representation collapse at aggressive downsampling rates without it, and a clean ablation demonstrating recovery with it.

Perlin noise masking is well motivated and validated with a spectral (PSD) analysis showing it better matches the intrinsic 1/f statistics of EM images compared to random masking, with a corresponding ablation showing improved downstream mIoU.

Reasonably comprehensive ablations (downsampling rate, masking ratio, deep supervision, masking strategy) and scaling analysis across resolutions (448–1024) showing consistent FLOPs/memory/throughput advantages while retaining near-parity mIoU with a ViT-MAE baseline.

Additional data-efficiency experiment (5%-100% of labels) suggesting the learned adaptive priors generalize better in low-annotation regimes, which is practically relevant for biomedical applications.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single dataset/domain (in-house EM images) and a single downstream task (FPW segmentation), so claims of general applicability to other high-resolution/dense-prediction domains are not empirically substantiated.

The only compared baseline is vanilla ViT-MAE; despite discussing SwinMAE and MixMAE at length in related work as directly relevant hierarchical/masked baselines, no quantitative comparison to these methods is provided, weakening the case that AFFMAE is preferable to existing hierarchical MIM alternatives.

Experiments use a single model/parameter scale (~22M); no scaling study (larger backbones, larger pretraining corpora) is provided to establish whether the efficiency-accuracy trade-off holds as scale increases.
No indication of variance/multiple seeds for the reported mIoU numbers, making it hard to assess whether the small differences (e.g., 0.5–0.7% mIoU gaps) are statistically meaningful.

The abstract's "Code available at" is left without an actual link in the reviewed manuscript, raising reproducibility concerns; combined with custom Triton kernels and an in-house unreleased dataset, independent verification would be difficult without released code/data.

The core contribution is largely an engineering/adaptation exercise (numerical stabilization, kernel re-implementation, deep supervision, task-specific masking) built directly on an existing architecture (AutoFocusFormer) rather than a new algorithmic idea, which should be judged as an applied/systems contribution rather than a fundamentally novel method — this recalibrates novelty expectations but should be made explicit by the authors.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: enabling in-domain, high-resolution self-supervised pretraining on desktop-class GPUs for privacy-sensitive biomedical labs, with a compelling clinical use case (podocyte foot process width estimation).

Solid engineering contribution: adapting AutoFocusFormer to be mask-agnostic while retaining hierarchical efficiency is a non-trivial combination that prior hierarchical MIM works (Swin-MAE, GreenMIM, MixMAE, HiViT) have struggled with due to dense-grid assumptions; this is clearly articulated and differentiated from prior art.

Multiple well-motivated technical components are each ablated and justified: deep supervision (with effective-rank and PCA diagnostics showing representational collapse is mitigated), Perlin-noise masking (justified via spectral PSD analysis matching biological image statistics), and a numerically stable exponential-kernel reformulation of the point-based decoder for mixed precision.

Strong empirical efficiency gains that are the core claim: 2x pretraining throughput and memory reduction over ViT-MAE, up to 5x fine-tuning speedup at 1024px, and scalability to higher resolutions where baselines OOM — these are convincingly demonstrated with FLOPs/memory/throughput tables and scaling curves (Fig. 4, Tables 3/5).

Downstream accuracy is competitive with ViT-MAE despite large efficiency gains, and AFFMAE notably outperforms other efficient hierarchical baselines (Swin-style: MixMAE, GreenMIM, HiViT, SimMIM) specifically on thin/fine structures (Slits IoU), which is argued and shown qualitatively (Fig. 5, Fig. 11-12) to stem from the adaptive vs. rigid-grid downsampling design.

Generalization is checked via supplementary results on three additional public EM benchmarks (Lucchi++, ISBI EM Challenge, Kasthuri++), where AFFMAE is competitive with or better than MAE and SimMIM, adding some evidence the gains are not overfit to the private FPW dataset.

Useful practical/systems contributions: custom Triton flash-style cluster attention kernels and a cached KNN lookup table for the decoder that yield measurable additional speedups (1.4-1.5x), addressing a known gap between theoretical FLOPs and realized wall-clock time in sparse/irregular architectures.
weaknesses: The primary FPW dataset (kidney EM) is private, and while public benchmarks are included in supplementary material, the main paper's central quantitative claims rest heavily on a non-reproducible, single-institution dataset; code availability is promised but not verifiable within the manuscript, limiting reproducibility.

AFFMAE's downstream accuracy gains over ViT-MAE are quite small (0.633 vs 0.630 mIoU at 1024px; 0.608 vs 0.606 at 512px) and largely within or near the reported standard deviations across seeds, so the 'matches MAE while being far more efficient' framing is more accurate than an outright accuracy improvement — this should be stated more conservatively, especially since some efficient baselines (SimMIM, HiViT) actually beat AFFMAE at certain resolutions/metrics (e.g., SimMIM's FPW MAE at 512/768, HiViT memory at 512).

Baseline compute comparisons are somewhat uneven: GreenMIM, HiViT, and MixMAE were pretrained on an H100 rather than the RTX 5090 used for AFFMAE/MAE/SimMIM (explicitly noted as 'not easily comparable'), which weakens the fairness of the headline efficiency comparisons against the full baseline set in Fig. 1/Table 3 despite the disclaimer.

The architecture is fundamentally an application of an existing backbone (AutoFocusFormer) and existing techniques (MAE, deformable cross-attention decoder from Deformable DETR/Mask2Former-style sampling, Perlin noise masking, deep supervision) recombined for a new setting; the core novelty is integration/engineering rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea, which should temper the significance claims somewhat despite the practical value.

Statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests or confidence intervals) is not reported for the close mIoU differences between AFFMAE and MAE/SimMIM, making it hard to assess whether the small numerical differences highlighted throughout (e.g., Slits IoU improvements) are meaningful versus noise given only 4 seeds.

The explainability discussion (token trajectories concentrating on GBM boundary) is interesting but purely qualitative/anecdotal, without any quantitative validation that token locations correlate with clinically relevant structures beyond a few visualized examples.

The downsampling-rate and masking-ratio ablations are conducted with a smaller 23M-parameter model at 300 epochs rather than the main 65M configuration used in the primary results, raising some question about whether the selected hyperparameters (ds=0.4, 50% masking) are optimal for the actual reported main-table models.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated practical problem: enabling in-domain, high-resolution self-supervised pretraining on desktop-class GPUs for privacy-sensitive, resource-constrained biomedical labs, with a clear real-world use case (kidney EM / foot process width estimation).

Technically sound integration of AutoFocusFormer's adaptive, off-grid token merging with the MAE paradigm, producing a genuinely mask-agnostic hierarchical encoder that avoids the dense-grid workarounds required by prior hierarchical MIM methods (SwinMAE, GreenMIM, MixMAE, HiViT).

Solid systems/engineering contributions: numerically stable softmax reformulation of inverse-distance decoder weighting, custom Triton FlashAttention-style cluster attention kernels, and an O(1) cached KNN lookup for the point-based decoder, each with measured speedups (1.5x/1.4x forward/backward for the decoder).

Thoughtful diagnostic analysis of representational collapse in sparse deep stages via PCA and normalized effective rank, well motivating the deep supervision design choice with clear supporting evidence (Figure 2).
Perlin-noise masking is justified not just empirically but through a principled spectral (PSD) analysis showing better alignment with the 1/f statistics of real EM images compared to random masking.

Broad empirical validation: main results on the FPW dataset across three resolutions plus additional public EM benchmarks (Lucchi++, Kasthuri++, ISBI EM Challenge) in the supplementary material, showing the method generalizes beyond the primary task.

Clearly demonstrated and consistently reported efficiency gains (2x pretraining throughput, ~2x memory reduction, up to 5x fine-tuning throughput at 1024px) while matching or slightly exceeding dense ViT-MAE segmentation accuracy, which is the core practical claim of the paper.
Good ablation coverage (downsampling rate, masking ratio, deep supervision variants, masking strategy) with quantitative and qualitative support (token visualization, effective rank plots).
weaknesses: The scope is narrowly demonstrated on EM/microscopy segmentation; no evidence is given that AFFMAE would work on natural images or other modalities, limiting claims of general applicability as a vision pretraining framework outside this niche (though the paper is explicit about this focus).

The headline performance improvement over dense ViT-MAE is small (e.g., 0.633 vs 0.630 mIoU at 1024px) and, given reported per-seed std (0.002-0.009), may not be clearly statistically significant in several resolution/metric combinations; the core contribution is efficiency parity rather than a decisive accuracy gain, which should be stated more conservatively.

The implementation details section states that 'All MIM models adopt the UperNet decoder... matched to the AFFMAE decoder's parameter count,' which appears to contradict/undercut the abstract's claim that the lightweight point-based decoder 'can be directly repurposed as a segmentation head'; it is unclear from the text whether the main Table 2 results for AFFMAE use its own decoder or UperNet, and no direct ablation isolates the segmentation benefit of the proposed decoder versus UperNet.

Cross-method comparisons are complicated by inconsistent hardware: GreenMIM, HiViT, and MixMAE were trained on H100 GPUs while the primary comparisons (ViT-MAE, SimMIM, AFFMAE) were run on an RTX 5090, muddying the throughput/memory comparisons in Table 3 and Figure 1 that are central to the paper's efficiency claims.

The architectural novelty is primarily integrative/engineering (combining an existing backbone, AutoFocusFormer, with MAE and a deformable point decoder) rather than a fundamentally new representation-learning idea; this is acceptable for an applied/systems contribution but should be clearly framed as such rather than emphasized as a new pretraining paradigm.

Ablation tables (Table 1a-1d) do not report variance/seeds unlike the main results table, making it harder to assess the robustness of the reported differences (e.g., 0.5947 vs 0.6009 for masking strategy).

Limited exploration of how the method scales with different backbone/parameter budgets beyond the ~65M and 23M configurations used for main results and ablations respectively, leaving open how conclusions generalize to smaller or larger models.
